To "beg the question" means to give an answer that uses the question. If I say, "Why is that guy ugly?" and you say, "Because he's unattractive," that's called begging the question. The phrase is commonly used incorrectly to say "which begs the question..." followed by some question that naturally follows.

In a logical argument, you are supposed to start with premises that everyone agrees on, and then use them to prove your point. Begging the question is when you start with a premise that assumes your point is already proven. For instance, if someone argues that you should believe their religion because their holy book says you should, this is begging the question. Accepting the premise (that the holy book is a credible source) assumes that the point is already proven (i.e., believing the religion).

For the record, I speak, of course, as an American, regarding the two movements in America. I hear people comparing the Civil Rights movement to the LGBT and marriage equality movements all the time. The LGBT struggle is one of acceptance for a lifestyle in which, if they aren't technically denied anything, they are only restricted in the ways they can obtain it. (I.e., they aren't denied the right to marry; they just can't get married in the manner they want.) While I'm not anti-gay, they aren't regarded as second-class citizens by our government, we aren't lynching them for looking at straight people seductively, and we aren't attacking them with water hoses and German shepherds. It insults me to compare "marriage equality" to the fight against Jim Crow, the fight for the right to vote, to use public restrooms, or to go to public schools of your choosing. Maybe I'm crazy, but I think it's messed up to compare the two. Change my view.

I assume anyone with the ability to flex their "power" in the name of the law is evil. They have the ability to bend the law to catch me for anything I do wrong, and we don't have a check or balance on them, at least not on the scale they have on us. "Justice," to me, is a joke. There is no such thing. On another note, even if they give me a ticket for doing something wrong, they're just trying to meet a quota so their department can get money. The money I pay for speeding should go to schools or a college fund to help those who need it, not to the police. There's a lot here; good luck changing my view. :)

Edit: I'll make this a bit clearer. I hate cops because they misuse power and act like it's their duty or right to do so.

Person1: OK, Mrs. Thomas. I finished cleaning up the leaves in the yard. Person2: Oh, thank you, James. Person1: I also swept the front steps and took out the garbage. Is there anything else I can help you with? Person2: Can you also take my dog Oscar for a walk? Person1: Sure. Person2: He is such a prince. Ever since I broke my leg, it has been so difficult to take care of things around the house. My daughter Leah helps out on Mondays and Tuesdays and my son Robbie on Thursdays, but I'm so happy you can come on Saturdays. Person1: Well, I appreciate the weekend work. I'm saving up to buy a bike so I can ride to my basketball practice. Person2: Will you still be able to work for me after you get your bike? Person1: Of course, but don't forget I'm away next weekend visiting my grandfather. My sister Allison will come by instead. Person2: OK.

We'd been wandering for what felt like years. I would have written down my adventures for later generations, but writing hadn't been invented yet. We set up camp near the mountain. It was supposed to offer defense, but against what, we weren't sure. The military hadn't been invented yet either.

Before long, we had developed a way to communicate. Then another camp sprang up a few tiles away from us. Another camp, then some more caravans to settle more cities. Things were moving at a hectic pace!

We learned how to work with metal, how to make buildings, and how to train soldiers. This was all within the first couple of weeks. It was like some... higher power was guiding our development, but I couldn't say for sure.

Wonders followed, then vehicles, enormous wars that almost engulfed the Medium map, and then a spaceship.

I've been alive on this planet for almost 10 weeks now, and I just hope I stay alive long enough to see our civilization expand to Alpha Centauri.

Historical definitions of Jewish identity have traditionally been based on halakhic definitions of matrilineal descent and halakhic conversions. Historical definitions of who is a Jew date back to the codification of the Oral Torah into the Babylonian Talmud, around 200 CE. Interpretations of sections of the Tanakh, such as Deuteronomy 7:1-5, by Jewish sages are used as a warning against intermarriage between Jews and Canaanites because "[the non-Jewish husband] will cause your child to turn away from Me and they will worship the gods (i.e., idols) of others." Leviticus 24:10 says that the son in a marriage between a Hebrew woman and an Egyptian man is "of the community of Israel." This is complemented by Ezra 10:2-3, where Israelites returning from Babylon vow to put aside their gentile wives and their children. Since the anti-religious Haskalah movement of the late 18th and 19th centuries, halakhic interpretations of Jewish identity have been challenged.
